problem: The list of escaped characters has a hole: it reads "turns &, , >, " and '" — the less-than sign is missing, so a student cannot tell that < is escaped (it was probably swallowed as an HTML tag).
fix: htmlspecialchars($s, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8') turns &, <, >, " and ' into HTML entities.

problem: "nl2br($s) inserts  before newlines" — the inserted text is missing, so the sentence states nothing.
The answer reads "User text may contain , > or &" — the < character is missing from the list, which is the very character that matters for script injection.
fix: User text may contain <, >, & or quotes. The function turns them into entities, so the browser shows text instead of running code. This helps prevent cross-site scripting.

problem: "In a double-quoted string, \d may be read as an escape, so you need extra backslashes" is wrong for \d. PHP only interprets known escapes (\n, \t, \\, \$, \", octal \1, \x, \u); an unknown sequence such as \d or \s is kept literally, backslash included. The real danger in double quotes is \1 (turned into an octal character) and a doubled backslash.
fix: Use single-quoted PHP strings for patterns: '/^[6-9]\d{9}$/'. In a double-quoted string PHP interprets escapes such as \n, \t, \\ and \1, so a pattern containing a backslash-digit sequence or a literal backslash can change; single quotes pass the pattern to PCRE unchanged.

problem: trim is described as removing "spaces and newlines", but its default character list also covers tabs, carriage returns, NUL and vertical tab; a student meeting a tab-padded value may think trim fails.
fix: trim($s) removes whitespace at both ends: spaces, tabs, newlines, carriage returns and NUL bytes.
